title: Embracing the Rave
summary: Stu Mackenzie and Joey Walker discuss the band’s improvised modular rave set, upcoming orchestral performances and the possibilities opened by playing without a fixed script.
transcript:
Stu Mackenzie and Joey Walker join Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 23 October 2025.

What a treat to be here. Thanks. Thank you. We're super thrilled.

And of course, as you mentioned at the top, Lauren, 27 albums in so far, not counting all of the, I suppose, unofficials and the bootlegs. And I guess throughout the course of 15 years, sort of have built a really vast catalogue of albums. But even more than that, something of a musical universe, I guess, the Gizzverse that people would know. And sometimes the albums that you produce, I suppose, well, always follow their own path. You've got your own label, p(doom) Records, which enables you to explore microtonal rock, thrash metal, long-form jazz improvisation and so much more. But of course, the most recent album, Phantom Island, that we were just listening to, came out in June with some beautiful orchestral arrangements, which is just stunning. And we couldn't be more excited to hear that you've got some electronic rave sets that you've been developing, too. This is going to be the first one tomorrow night in Australia at Fed Square, DJ Merve supporting. It's free, and it starts at 7pm, so I'm sure it's going to be hard to find a spot at the front. But if you get there early enough, maybe you'll be lucky. But yeah, we're so excited. And we want to ask you about where this idea was born, this new chapter of electronic rave music.

Sick. It's probably been... Thanks for the very epic intro as well. We just make music mostly, which makes sense. But it's been something that has been coming together for a few years. And then also simmering away in the background for probably quite a lot of years before that as well. And I think we probably had this goal to try and figure out how to make live improvised techno with six people, which seems hard and is extremely hard. It actually is hard. So I think we're starting to find the spot within that universe that makes sense for us to [Unclear audio at 00:02:18.120–00:02:27.700], I think.

By sort of coincidence, I guess the week that you're planning your first local rave set, Tame Impala dropped their new rave album as well. It feels like, I don't know, there's something in the air at the moment. Were you sort of channeling a feeling of needing to dance and release energy?

I feel like... I mean, yes and no. I feel like there's kind of... It has, as you said, been simmering away. Like Butterfly 3000 was like a fully, like there wasn't a single acoustic instrument on that record. It's all just like synthesizers. And then, but it wasn't a dance album. And then I guess the [Unclear audio at 00:03:05.280–00:03:11.500] remix album was like, it was amazing. The artists that kind of came aboard for that, which is crazy.

And then, yeah, I feel like over the last kind of post-pandemic... During the pandemic, I got into Eurorack modular synthesizing, which is kind of something that has been an endgame for me for a really long time. That's the format. For people out there, it's just like the funny-looking synth with heaps of cables on it. That's that, that thing. It's synthesizer guts, cables on the outside. Yeah.

And then, so, I guess during, like, a normal Gizzard show, I would kind of have my little Eurorack synth on stage and I'd kind of contribute in that way. And then we started to kind of... We made the record The Silver Cord, which kind of was this, I don't know, like Frankenstein genre of electronic music, which kind of ended up being whatever that was and stuff. And then I guess, like, um, Stu kind of inevitably... I was like, man, this modular thing seems like... [Unclear audio at 00:04:04–00:04:12]

And I was like, nah, it's boring. Stop talking about it all the time. I mean, yeah.

And then classic Stu just kind of started from nothing and now could have a modular synthesis YouTube channel dedicated to it.

We heard that it's hard to find you outside of exploring synthesizers at the moment. You're spending most of your days in front of them. I guess you have said that your recent obsession with Eurorack modular synthesis feels like discovering guitar as a teenager all over again. Is that right?

Yeah. Yeah, it does. I had this realization that the feeling is really similar to when I first started playing guitar, and it just felt like the universe was massive and that you could do anything with this instrument. And that's how I remember feeling as a teenager, first learning to play guitar. And I think that I have that same feeling now and it's, it's good. I kind of try and chase that, actually, making music. And it's cool when you latch onto something like that. I remember when we started doing microtonal music, there was a similar feeling of, like, kind of the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow sort of thing. Um, but yeah, we try to chase that thing.

And what does it look like and sound like in the studio with you when you're, yeah, messing with these cables? I sort of have an impression of what Eurorack modular synthesis looks like, but in your world, what does it look like? Is it controlled chaos?

Really funny. It's like our studio is just a night... Like, it's like a crime scene. It's so hectic. Our sound guy who lives in Byron Bay just drove, like, arrived today for the show tomorrow, and he just walked in and he was just like, oh my God. But yeah, it's, uh, we all are kind of, um, on a table, a big table and we kind of have our A-frame modular, each of our synths kind of A-frame together. So like me and Stu are back to back. It's a giant pyramid. Yeah, it's a pyramid.

And then Ambrose and Cookie are kind of joined, and Lucas is on the end of the table as well. And then Cavs, the drummer, is on the kit. And then he was kind of the last to the party where he was kind of just like, shut up. And then, uh, but then Stu's just built him a little kind of like drum machine kind of Eurorack kit. And Cavs just like, he's like, all right, all right. Kind of like walked into the studio and like caught him just like trying to get like a patch cable. And he turned around and he was so like embarrassed. But no, we're all, we're all there.

So we're kind of like... The thing, I guess, is like, we kind of have our songs that we're playing that, you know, would be from The Silver Cord. Or some other songs that we're kind of retrofitting to this setup. Um, and they're kind of in a very simple form. Like it's kind of like maybe a key melody that everyone's receiving, but that is kind of maybe like the binding sinew to the song. But outside of that, it's completely kind of improvised in the time, like in the moment. And like the, the great thing with modular is that it's very generative. So you can kind of... And, you know, we don't want to go into a tech deep dive here, but essentially it's really good at kind of manifesting and kind of creating melody and rhythm and whatever, pulling it out of thin air, really.

So it's kind of like a dance with each other, of how we interact in that moment, and it's hard enough doing that with one person, let alone two, but with, like, six people doing it, it's a lot. It's like, it's a dance to kind of like let things breathe and all that stuff. So it's been really good. And I feel like we're kind of at a really exciting point with it all. And it also feels infinite. I feel like, in terms of where we can take it... But yeah, we're nervous for tomorrow, but we're excited.

It sounds like there's a lot of adrenaline involved in general.

Totally. Totally. Yeah.

And I guess in addition to, yeah, this rave set, you've been touring, I guess, these three sort of distinct shows simultaneously, the rock orchestral and these electronic rave sets. You'll be back in December for the orchestra show on December 12. And then there's the next night as well, which is more of a rock show. Can you tell us the difference, I guess, between them from your perspective, maybe in terms of even like the sort of preparation and performance aspects behind them?

The orchestra shows are probably the, I feel like for us as a band, they're probably furthest from what we're used to. We have to play to charts and we've got, you know, 30 odd people behind us who are playing to a script, which is not the way we tend to operate. So we've kind of worked out a really fun way of doing it though, because we've done quite a few of the orchestra kind of shows now. But yeah, we have to kind of be more of a cog in the machine. And that's fun. That's fun. It's actually discipline. It's a bit of... It's different. It's discipline. It requires discipline.

Whereas the usual show is not discipline-based, you know, that's not... It's actually a lack of discipline that's what usually works the best with the band.

And one thing I realised as well with the, the like kind of, um, the orchestra show versus like a traditional Gizzard show is when we were kind of on tour a month or two ago in America doing like kind of primarily the orchestra stuff. But then we'd kind of have, um, a normal rock show in between and you kind of like going into the orchestra thing, it was very unfamiliar. We didn't know what to expect. We were all very nervous, like dealing with these, like, you know, professional musicians and stuff like that. But once we kind of got over that initial kind of feeling, and, like, realizing, oh, it's actually kind of... That is what it is... Once we're there, we kind of don't have to really worry about it. Like the variables aren't as much of a thing.

And then going into a normal Gizzard show, I was like, oh wow, the amount of work, I guess mental work, at least how I feel going into a Gizzard show, because it's so last minute, every set's different. You know, tonight Stu will be like, we're going to play this song. Like, I don't, I don't even know what that song was called. Like, I don't, you know, I haven't heard that song in however long. So it's kind of, there's so much kind of like energy, um, put into a normal Gizzard show, um, that I think at the end of the day really pays off for us and hopefully for the audience, like that kind of frenetic, chaotic feel to it. But like, um, it was interesting to see that kind of duality between like this kind of very regimented orchestral thing and a normal Gizzard show. It was cool. It's refreshing, I think.

And you worked with, I think it was conductor, Sarah Hicks, and there's the composer and music director, Chad Kelly, as well on the orchestra tour. How did they sort of change how you think about your own music?

Yeah, I've actually known Chad for quite a few years. Our wives are friends, actually. And so I met Chad just sort of at dinner parties and stuff like that. Chad's a Manchester chap who married an Aussie, but he's a conductor and a, um, composer and such an incredible musician. And we would kind of get together on these like dinner party dates and, and talk about like microtonal music and like dorky stuff like that. And it was, it was really rad. But we do very much exist on very opposite ends of the kind of musical spectrum. I think we kind of are both interested in deeply dorky stuff, which is where we connected. But I'm, like, a musical idiot and he's like a smart musical person. So we just... But we fight, we meet in the middle.

But anyway, um, we, we had some opportunities to play some, uh, live shows in the States with an orchestra. And the idea was to kind of retrofit the back catalog and do some, yeah, shows with like, you know, some like amazing top orchestras in the States. And of course we were just like, well, we have to take that. What a cool opportunity. So the first person I called was Chad to get his take on the whole thing. And I think after speaking with him and after brainstorming a little bit, it just became obvious that if we want to do one show, we may as well do a tour. And if we're going to do a tour, we may as well make an album. And so Chad really helped with like the whole process. And he, he wrote the charts for Phantom Island and what became of that.

And, um, and yeah, he's touring with us in, in Europe as the conductor for the shows.

And Australia as well.

And Australia as well.

And Sarah Hicks did the U.S. stuff and she's so incredible as well. Um, I have so much respect for conductors now. I just never knew what they were doing with their little magic wands. But now I feel like I do, and it's an incredible job of being able to communicate with all of the different musicians, and especially working with a rock band that they have to kind of understand what we are all doing. It's like different, it's like understanding of different languages.

Yeah.

It's beautiful to hear you communicate, coming from different places, but yeah, finding that middle ground.

And the, yeah, Sarah is such an amazing conductor. She had this ability to be able to, um, relay this information to every, every person in a different language, essentially one by one. It's very cool. Very, very impressive skill.

And you've also been playing in some pretty special places in Europe recently. Back in May you played, I think it was a former prison in Lithuania that's been converted into like a music venue there. Can we ask about sort of the logistics of that? And also I guess what the selection process is like for choosing these locations for your shows?

I mean, the logistics... Kind of like, let's, like, do a tour that's kind of destination-based. And in terms of like the intensity of what that tour was like, it was like, you know, we did five different places. Each place was three nights in each place. So for us, it was kind of pretty low impact, which was really nice, to just be in a place. And they were really amazing places. So actually it was kind of like good for the old mental health.

Because you'd be accustomed to traveling sort of rapidly to places.

It's just like the stereotype of just like waking up in like a car park type thing in the bus behind the venue. And you have no idea where you are. Yeah, it's kind of weird. But yeah, that was really cool. And I think it was just like, yeah, I don't know. It was just really, really amazing. It was like the venues brought so much like energy to the shows. And like you kind of could just draw from like, we did the one sort of like Lycabettus Hill, which was like the second highest point in Athens, other than the hill that the Acropolis is on. And just like up there at sunset, it was just like insane how cool it was.

Incredible.

Briefly, we would like to sort of flip to talking about some of the recordings that you've been working on. And of course, Phantom Island was the most recent record written during the same sessions as Flight b741. You've described the process of making Phantom Island as sort of adding a new color and energy to the songs. You've talked a bit about your experience with, I suppose, the, yeah, the musical directors and the composers, Sarah Hicks and Chad Kelly. But can you talk a little bit more about, yeah, the sort of themes and ideas that you're exploring on this record?

I mean, yeah, musically, it was very cool to work with an orchestra. I mean, it does actually feel like you're painting with, like, let's say a different set of colors, especially to a rock band. And the kind of the stuff that we were doing on that record was pretty bare bones. Like, we were kind of thinking back to basics. There's no guitar pedals, sort of just, you know, we were kind of saying the music that comes out of your fingertips. It's like just trying to be simple and trying to be kind of the organic version of the guitar and that sort of thing. And having so many different sort of colors and sounds to play with in the orchestra is very, very cool. It's very cool. But, yeah, Chad Kelly arranged, like, amazing stuff for it.

I feel like, like, thematically, you know, I mean, yeah, like, it's just kind of, it's pretty, like, it's pretty obvious. But it's like, yeah, it's kind of just talking about just, like, up to where we are now. Like, just kind of how transient, I guess, our lives have become and stuff. And, you know, we all have families for the most part. And, yeah, so it's kind of like a little bit of an examination of that kind of thing. But, yeah. Felt pretty honest and personal for a record for us, I think. And we're probably challenging ourselves and each other to see how kind of, like, earnest you could kind of get away with on a rock track like that.

Excellent. I guess in terms of, yeah, challenging each other or challenging yourselves, perhaps. In the past, you've said that [Unclear audio at 00:16:48.100–00:16:54.940], you deliberately make yourself uncomfortable creatively, like using cheap gear. You're forcing yourselves into these unfamiliar genres as well. Is that still the case? Or are there sort of other strategies or techniques you use to maintain creativity and your sort of prolific output?

Well, I mean, for this record, I definitely didn't tell Chad or any of the orchestral players at the time. But we mixed down to an 8-track cassette tape, which is, like, a very cool machine from the 80s, which is extremely broken. But, yeah, thinking about, like, an extremely hi-fi, big orchestra and, you know, we recorded it properly this time. By the way, we mixed down to, like, a tiny cassette. And that actually felt like a huge challenge. And it was kind of the game. The game was to see how you could get the tape to sound as good as possible, actually. So it's just, I don't know why I do this.

There's also a little bit of a kind of subvert... Trying to subvert doing an orchestral record. You know, it comes with its own kind of... Not baggage, but it has a feeling to it. You're like, okay, that's that. And very often, like, when a band or bands do that, it can kind of just, like, really not be their best work. So I feel like there was a little bit of a subversion into, like, let's, like, make this, like, garage-ify it. You know what I mean? And, like, kind of... Which is cool. I think it kind of shows off, like, that. Like, if it was this ultra hi-fi kind of thing, I just think it might have, like, I don't know, like, lost a bit of its soul. Or at least a bit of our kind of spirit. I think that it's always trying to inject the Gizzard thing into it.

It was also genuinely a very, very hard record to finish. And I think it had a bit to do with the, yeah, the combination of kind of, like, we were sort of in blues band formation, really. And fusing that with kind of an orchestral, you know, a small orchestra was, like, I think we had, like, 30-odd people in the studio for the orchestral recording. So it was really hard to make that fit. And I think this slightly sadistic way of mixing a record kind of made it make sense, actually. And it made it live in the same world.

And I think also back to your kind of initial question in terms of, like, impetus, creative impetus or whatever. But, I mean, like, b741 and Phantom Island, kind of same session in terms of the original tracks that were on both those albums. But that was kind of a response to this kind of little scene of albums that we'd had, which were very jammy and nebulous. And, like, the process was, like, a lot of kind of post-production distillation of these huge, expansive jams that we'd do. And then kind of, like, trying to form these, build these songs out of it. So it was, like, okay, once we'd gotten through that, we're, like, we just want to make, like, a song with, like, a couple of chords. And that's what that is.

And then so now coming out the other side of that, everyone has, like, absurd modular synthesizers. Because, you know what I mean? So it is that thing. It's, like, we are chasing kind of, like, once something's cauterized, we kind of try and do the opposite. Or what feels the most exciting.

I guess there's been, is it 27 albums in, like, the last 14, 15 years or so? You've covered, as I mentioned earlier, so many genres from, like, thrash metal, synth pop, jazz, electronic rave. Is there a genre you're excited or perhaps also are you scared to attempt?

I think for the most part we probably aren't thinking in terms of genre. I mean, maybe we are occasionally. I think we are genuinely chasing that feeling. We're chasing the dragon of the hard thing, probably, or the thing that would make us, yeah, sort of scared a little bit or motivated enough to, yeah, just, I don't know.

It kind of can kind of manifest in, like, in a technical, like, side. So, like, you know, being scared of the learning curve that comes with learning how to, you know, use a modular synth. Like, and, you know, it's kind of one of those things where... I've kind of had a bit of a... I have a background in dance music or electronic music. And Stu's just, like, got hyper-focused kind of thing. But, like, a lot of the other guys, it's, like, I guess we're doing modular synthesis now. So there's the kind of trying to inject some form of learning curve that is kind of cool to try and tackle. And then there's also, yeah, and it just might be, I don't know.

I think it's, like, trying to put in these kind of restrictions, but, like, kind of barriers within something, within a framework that kind of, like, once we kind of decide, okay, cool, this album might be metal, or it might be ultra-proggy, or it might be electronic. We kind of just, like, set these kind of things. Like, there's all channels or lanes in between that where it actually kind of, like... If we try and narrow...

Yeah, make it make sense.

Make it make sense.

And once we kind of, like, realise what that is, that's when we're, like, let's make the album. And then it kind of happens really quickly because it's almost, like, working out what we're not doing. Sometimes there can be a lot of time before we sort of start anything or we just talk about it and figure out what exactly the intent is. It's also just sometimes fun to just burn the house down and start again. And, yeah, I think there's an element of that, too.

Excellent. Well, it is so thrilling to be a fan of your work because there is always that sense of exhilaration, excitement and, you know, entering into the unknown. I suppose something that we wanted to talk to you about before we let you go is the community that you have really built through your tireless work ethic. I suppose weirdoswarm.org is one of the places where people track the shows they've attended. They organise meet-ups. They run charity events and participate in an annual gift exchange called Gizzmas. It's a beautiful community that you've built over so many years. We were just kind of wondering how much you get to engage with that at all, like, and where that sort of fits within your, yeah, I suppose, working schedules.

For me, you know, like, when you talk about, yeah, that stuff, it is pretty abstract for the most part. It is actually quite a strange and sort of, like, unreal concept to sort of, like, truly understand. And I feel like the thing I have said before, especially when we were talking about the record b741, which had a lot of flying on planes metaphors, but a lot of it does feel like being in an aeroplane. If you actually think about the fact that you are in the sky, it's quite... You actually might have a panic attack. And I think, like, being, playing to, you know, the kind of audiences that we're lucky enough to play to now, you actually have to... I have to abstract myself from it because it just actually doesn't do any good to think too hard about what the whole, the broader ecosystem is.

However, I do really like talking to people. And I'll always try and, like, chat with folks and kind of get a sense of what is going on on the ground.

Yeah, I think we do.

And that's when it feels real.

Yeah.

I think we do, yeah, like, that is our interaction. It's kind of like, yeah, we like to hear and, like, because we do have a lot of people, you know, like, kind of across the world who, you know, might be kind of, like, figures within the kind of Giz community, Giz fan community, who we, like, we honestly do talk to and, like, have, you know, like, they talk to our managers, we talk to them, like, we also, you know, there's a kind of exchange of relationship.

But for the most part, I think, like, as to just the whole kind of the lore, like, L-O-R-E lore of the whole thing, it's, like, I think if we were to actually kind of stop and engage, it actually kind of wouldn't – it would kind of cease to exist, you know. And I think, like, we just kind of let it exist and do – it's there because we haven't – we're not engaging with it, you know. We're just kind of doing our thing. And we just like making music with each other. It's kind of as simple as that. We actually just like being in the same room as each other and making music together. And that's, like, that's the thing.

I believe it's being live-streamed as well, isn't it?

Yeah, we try to live-stream as many of our shows as we can. We do it on YouTube for free. Tune in.
